claims.text: Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 exhibits negligible hardening and good radiation resistance under energetic-particle exposure.
Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 develops Cr-V-rich precipitates near 8 dpa.
Adding approximately 2–4 at.% Hf to nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 will suppress Cr-V-rich precipitate formation near 8 dpa.
The 2–4 at.% Hf addition will preserve low irradiation hardening.
The 2–4 at.% Hf addition will preserve the alloy's radiation resistance.
The 2–4 at.% Hf addition will preserve practical bulk manufacturability.
Temperatures of 300–500°C are typical of fusion first-wall or divertor service.
Hf addition will produce stable, finely dispersed Hf-rich clusters in the W-based matrix.
The Hf-rich clusters will act as sinks for vacancies and other radiation-induced defects.
Hf-rich clusters will capture and immobilize irradiation-generated point defects and dislocation loops.
Immobilization of point defects and dislocation loops will inhibit nucleation and growth of Cr-V-rich precipitates.
A minor Hf addition will not significantly increase alloy complexity relevant to manufacturability.
After irradiation, the Hf-modified alloy will have a markedly lower Cr-V-rich precipitate density than unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11.
After irradiation, the Hf-modified alloy will show less hardening than unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11.
The Hf-modified alloy will retain radiation resistance and manufacturability comparable to the unmodified alloy.
Unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11 shows a modest increase in hardening under irradiation at 8 dpa and 300–500°C.
The proposed benefit is expected only up to 8 dpa and within 300–500°C.
Exposure outside the specified dose or temperature limits could cause phase-stability or processing problems.

contradictions.description: The initial-state field says the unmodified alloy exhibits negligible hardening, whereas the baseline field says it shows a modest increase in hardening under the stated exposure.
